title: About the Facilitator
text: Hi folks. My name is Nathan and I am an assistant professor in the Howard University School of Education and the HU Center for Applied Data Science and Analytics (CADSA). I am looking forward to learning together and I encourage you to contribute your expertise during our time.

title: Quantitative Section of the 2026 HUSOE ELPS Methods and Data Institute
text:
Thank you for joining us. This site is to support your learning during this Quantitative Section of the 2026 Howard University ELPS Methods and Data Institute. My name is Professor Nathan Alexander and I will be today’s facilitator.
Today’s workshop is about quantitative data collection and analysis.
For this workshop, I will take a Computational Studies in Education (CSIE) approach. CSIE is an interdisciplinary field that uses computational methods — like data analysis, modeling, and machine learning — to study how people learn, behave, and interact in social and educational contexts. At its core, it blends ideas from education, the social sciences, and computer science.
Instead of relying only on traditional paper-based methods that focus on small-scale surveys or interviews, computational studies uses data to drawn various conclusions that extend beyond what is taught in most introductory and intermediate courses in statistics. In particular, this field works with large-scale and complex data when engage in quantitative analysis.
Given our education focus, we’ll focus on survey methods and I’ll introduce some interesting tools and methods for computational text analysis – which, with time and care, can be applied to your interviews and focus groups.
For today’s institute, we will use an alternative to SPSS known as R. The software platform is free and online, meaning you will not need to download anything to your computer. However, if you’d like to get the software set up locally, instructions are here.

title: Quantitative Section of the 2026 HUSOE ELPS Methods and Data Institute
text:
Learning Outcomes
By the end of this workshop, you will be able to:

Describe basic data analysis workflows using real-world educational data
Produce a technical reports using what is called an R Markdown (in Quarto)

Import, clean, and visualize data using tidyverse tools

Formulate and interpret equity-focused research questions using data

Extend these methods to support your dissertation research and analysis

title: About the Facilitator
text:
Teaching
At Howard, I teach a variety of courses across the School of Education and CADSA. I hold a joint appointment in the Department of Curriculum and Instruction, where I teach math methods and international education, and in the Program in Applied Data Science and Analytics, where I teach courses in computation, probability, and statistical modeling.

title: About the Facilitator
text:
Research
Broadly, my research focuses on three strands: (1) the role of “context” in probability, statistics, and mathematical modeling, (2) how humans learn to use increasingly complex information to quantify things across the lifespan, and (3) Black diaspora studies in educator preparation. Starting in early childhood education all the way up to elderhood, I am also interested in how quantification informs decision-making, perspectives on the world, and critical computational practices1 in informal and non-traditional settings.
Here are a few examples by strand (click on the text):

The role of “context” in probability, statistics, and mathematical modeling
How humans learn to use complex information to quantify things
Black diaspora studies in educator preparation

title: About the Facilitator
text:
Research Lab
At Howard, I direct the Quantitative Histories Workshop, which is a computational curriculum collective and community-centered teaching and learning lab.
At our core, our lab integrates high-dimensional data sets to analyze problems over long periods of time, like centuries. We then engage in what is called “uncertainty quantification” to test models that describe how much error we think is present in both our data and analysis.
We also engage in spatial data analysis and Black archival studies in our analysis of primary documents that relate to the use of mathematics, statistics, and data to advance racial, economic, and spatial justice.

Here is some of our work in spatial data analysis.
Here is a talk about our archival work on Black mathematicians.

You can find out more about me and my lab’s research online here.
